newsitem.title: USA: Analysis shows Dole edging Clinton in online world.
newsitem.headline: Analysis shows Dole edging Clinton in online world.

text.p: While most polls gave President Clinton a slight edge in the first presidential debate, reaction in cyberspace favoured Republican challenger Bob Dole, according to an analysis by a University of Florida professor.

Advertising professor Marilyn Roberts, an expert on political communication, analysed political message groups on America Online, as well as political media Internet sites and the candidates' own World Wide Web sites after the first debate Oct. 6.

"My preliminary findings show that Dole has a higher approval percentage on-line than in the CNN and Gallup polls. I feel this is related to the make up of the users of America Online, but I also think that many people feel Dole did a better job than they expected in the first debate," she said.
Roberts said America Online members tend to be more male and more conservative that the population as a whole.

Roberts said some users of America Online who sent pro-Dole messages after the debate criticised television coverage for providing a kind of "visual bias" for example by showing Clinton's reaction rather than Dole's face when Dole was reacting to Clinton's comments.
This was similar to criticism of media coverage of Clinton's 1992 presidential debate with President George Bush, when Bush was shown looking at his watch, Roberts said.
She said the opinion of last week's vice presidential debate closely reflected that of the presidential debate.

"This is a brand new medium," Roberts said. "It's as if we were in 1952 with the birth of television political advertising with (former President Dwight) Eisenhower and (Adlai) Stevenson, or in the radio era and the impact that FDR's (former President Franklin Delano Roosevelt's) fireside chats had on the American public.
